B & W GROUP LIMITED
 
 
 
STRATEGIC REPORT
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31 DECEMBER 2025

Principal Activities & Change of Ownership

In September 2025, B & W Group Ltd. (“the Company”) and its subsidiary undertakings were acquired in full by Harman International Industries, Incorporated, a wholly owned subsidiary of Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd.
 
The core strategy remains focused on consolidating the Company’s leadership position within the global premium audio sector. Operating as a consumer-centric business, this strategy dictated operational focus throughout the financial year ended 31 December 2025 and remains the primary driver of future growth.

Business Review and Key Performance Drivers

During the financial year, the Company successfully expanded its premium product portfolio and leveraged strategic brand partnerships:
- Product Launches & Brand Partnerships: The Company brought to market the Px7 S3 and Px8 S2 headphone models, continuing its high-profile collaboration with McLaren Group Ltd. Additionally, a limited-edition 800 Series loudspeaker was launched in partnership with Abbey Road Studios, reinforcing the brand's heritage in professional audio.
- Licensing Revenue: The Company continues to monetise its patented acoustic technology through licensing arrangements with premium automotive and television manufacturers. This portfolio generated strong, highly profitable revenue streams during the period, with the Company capturing the full economic benefits of expanded contractual agreements.
- Brand Marketing & Awareness: Capitalising on its global brand ambassador partnership, the Company sustained targeted marketing campaigns throughout 2025 to scale brand awareness, drive digital engagement, and capture broader consumer demographics.

Research, Development and Manufacturing Capital Expenditure

Substantial investment in Research and Development (R&D) remains a cornerstone of the Company’s competitive advantage. This capital deployment sustains the brand's critical acclaim, drives strong sales demand, and underpins innovation within the premium wireless speaker segment. The Directors remain committed to ensuring that all future product pipelines maintain the premium quality benchmarks synonymous with the Bowers & Wilkins brand.

Simultaneously, the Company continued to modernise its global manufacturing infrastructure. Capital was deployed into advanced process automation and robotics across the primary operational facilities in Worthing, UK, and Zhuhai, China, enhancing production efficiency and quality control.

Outlook and Resilience

The Directors consider the Company to be exceptionally well-positioned to compete within the premium audio and high-performance headphone markets. Over the next 18 months, growth is projected to be driven by a robust pipeline of planned product launches, accelerating e-commerce volumes, increased website traction generated using celebrity endorsements, and the realisation of post-acquisition synergy benefits.

Strategic investments in manufacturing capacity, digital infrastructure, and global distribution networks ensure the Company possesses the necessary operational scale, inventory depth, and financial liquidity to capitalise on higher-than-forecast market demand. Conversely, the cost base retains sufficient flexibility to scale back operational expenditure should macroeconomic conditions dictate.

Financial Risk Management: Foreign Exchange

The Company's financial results remain exposed to foreign exchange volatility. The Directors actively monitor this risk and consider that the Company's structural natural hedges—whereby United States Dollar (USD) denominated sales are closely matched against USD-denominated procurement costs—provide robust mitigation against normal currency fluctuations while maintaining commercial flexibility.

Strategic Review and Operational Drivers

- Premium Capital Allocation: Production volumes at our flagship Worthing plant increased by 8.6%, reflecting a deliberate operational pivot toward high-margin, top-end premium manufacturing.
- Product Lifecycle Transition: The scaling of Worthing facilities was a critical phase of our operational gearing strategy ahead of the next-generation refresh of our flagship acoustic loudspeaker portfolio.
- Flagship Launch Horizon: Tooling, capacity adjustments, and pre-launch manufacturing validation are progressing aligned to the formal market introduction scheduled for September 2026.
- Market Expansion & Customer Acquisition: Going forward, production strategies will increasingly support our targeted expansion into the premium headphone sector.
- Brand Amplification Strategy: This category expansion is designed to drive global brand exposure, capture broader market demographics, and create cross-selling pathways back to our core high-fidelity audiophile portfolio.

Environmental and Sustainable Operations

The Company is committed to minimising the environmental impact of its global operations and downstream product lifecycles. The Directors maintain rigorous oversight frameworks to ensure the Company, its manufacturing facilities, and its global supply chain comply fully with all applicable UK, European, and international environmental legislation.

Streamlined Energy and Carbon Reporting

B & W Group Ltd is committed to sustainability and environmental responsibility at its manufacturing plant on Dale Road in Worthing. Recognising the impacts of its operations on the planet, the company has embedded sustainability at the core of its activities at this site and aligns with the broader Harman Group’s ambitious science-based sustainability targets.

GHG emissions were calculated using the UK Government GHG Conversion Factors for Company Reporting 2025. B & W Group Ltd’s total energy consumption for the reporting period was 5,715,031 kWh (2024 - 3,960,387 kWh). B & W Group Ltd’s total emissions using location-based reporting for the reporting period was 1,049 t CO2e (2024 - 822 t CO2e). Total emissions following a market-based approach for the reporting period were 1,884 t CO2e (1,339 t CO2e). The intensity ratio selected was tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalents per turnover (t CO2e/$m). The intensity ratio for the reporting period was 11.02t CO2e/$m (2024 - 7.48t CO2e/$m).

As required by the SECR scheme, B & W Group Ltd reports on energy efficiency measures implemented during
Page 2
 
B & W GROUP LIMITED
 
 
 
STRATEGIC REPORT (CONTINUED)
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31 DECEMBER 2025

the year. At the Worthing Dale Road manufacturing plant, the company has progressed several initiatives to support its carbon reduction objectives and contribute to Harman’s Group-wide emissions reduction goals:
• Establishing a Carbon Steering Group with a dedicated action plan for the plant, focusing on key areas such as Scope 1 & 2 emissions, materials and services, waste, and operational enablers.
• B & W Group Ltd are continually improving their environmental data collection to increase accuracy and move away from the EEIO carbon reporting methodology for more detailed reporting of emissions by supplier, client, and operational field team.
• Actively exploring the transition to 100% renewable electricity at the plant and considering other low-carbon technologies, such as the electrification of heating and the use of biogas, although specific implementation plans have not yet been finalised.
• Transitioning where feasible to electric technologies for plant operations, including the continued adoption of electric vehicles and equipment.

These measures support B & W Group Ltd’s efforts to reduce the environmental footprint of its Worthing manufacturing operations while advancing Harman’s commitment to long-term emissions reductions and carbon neutrality.

Key regulatory compliance frameworks integrated into the Company’s operations include:

- Product Material Compliance: Strict adherence to the Restriction of Hazardous Substances (RoHS) Directive, and the Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of Chemicals (REACH) regulations, ensuring all premium audio components and finishes meet stringent chemical safety standards.
- Lifecycle and Waste Management: Full compliance with the Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment (WEEE) Regulations to support responsible product end-of-life recycling and circular economy principles.
- Energy Efficiency and Carbon Reduction: Active adherence to the UK Energy Savings Opportunity Scheme (ESOS) and streamlined carbon reporting requirements, utilising data to drive efficiency across operations.

The Directors treat environmental sustainability as an iterative operational objective. The Board continuously reviews internal manufacturing processes, logistics networks, and supplier sustainability standards against long-term corporate responsibility goals to reduce carbon intensity and waste.

Risk Management Framework and Governance

Operating as a premium developer and manufacturer of proprietary and third-party produced audio equipment, the Company is exposed to a variety of operational, strategic, and financial risks. The Board of Directors retains ultimate responsibility for the Company’s risk management framework and is actively involved in identifying, evaluating, and mitigating exposures across the global supply chain, production facilities, intellectual property assets, and product quality benchmarks.

Following the acquisition in September 2025, the Directors are actively engaged in aligning the Company’s internal risk management controls, governance structures, and reporting methodologies with the global compliance policies and best practices of its new parent group, Harman International Industries.

Beyond ongoing integration and alignment initiatives, the Company's core risk management policies and operational controls remained consistent throughout the financial year, with no material changes implemented between the balance sheet date and the date of approval of these financial statements.

Supply Chain and Logistics Risk Management

Disruptions within the supply chain can lead to component shortages, production delays, and compromised product quality. Given the global scale and physical length of the Company’s supply chain, it remains inherently vulnerable to geopolitical tension, freight bottlenecks, and supplier insolvency. Any resulting inability to meet market demand or maintain strict build standards could negatively affect customer satisfaction, retailer relationships, and the premium reputation of the Bowers & Wilkins brand.

 
Page 3
 
B & W GROUP LIMITED
 
 
 
STRATEGIC REPORT (CONTINUED)
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31 DECEMBER 2025

The Company mitigates these exposures through a rigorous supplier selection and governance framework. Partners are vetted based on technical capability, production capacity, quality assurance, cost efficiency, and strict compliance with environmental and labour standards. Wherever commercially viable, the Company establishes long-term strategic partnerships, continuously monitors delivery performance, reviews the financial viability of key vendors, and maintains comprehensive business interruption insurance.

To buffer against short-term volatility, the Company maintains formal safety stock policies, strategically holding buffer inventories of critical sub-assemblies and long-lead components at key points in the manufacturing network. To counteract broader logistics volatility, the Company uses advanced demand forecasting to secure freight capacity ahead of peak production cycles. Furthermore, following the acquisition, the Company is actively leveraging the global procurement networks, carrier agreements, and logistics scale of the Harman Group to increase supply chain resilience and secure preferential transport capacity.

The Company’s manufacturing presence relies on a footprint of core production facilities, notably its primary operational sites in Worthing, UK, and Zhuhai, China. Any prolonged unscheduled downtime at these facilities whether caused by catastrophic machinery breakdowns, natural disasters, localised power interruptions, or critical utility failures could restrict production output. This disruption could materially impair the Company's capacity to fulfill trade orders, meet retail customer demands, and protect its standard revenue streams.

The Directors proactively manage production vulnerabilities through formalised business continuity and disaster recovery frameworks designed to protect operations. The engineering and facilities teams enforce structured preventative maintenance protocols and invest in advanced process automation to reduce hardware failure rates.

Furthermore, the Company protects its financial position against severe operational crises by maintaining comprehensive, high-limit property damage and business interruption insurance policies. Following the integration with the new parent company, the Board is reviewing industrial resilience strategies to leverage the broader network infrastructure of the Harman Group for potential capacity support should local issues arise.

Intellectual Property and Brand Infringement Risk Management

The Company’s market differentiation and premium brand positioning depend heavily on its proprietary technologies, industrial designs, and acoustic engineering processes. Unauthorised reproduction, counterfeiting, or intellectual property (IP) infringement by third parties could dilute the Bowers & Wilkins brand equity, erode market share, and impair high-margin licensing revenue streams across automotive and consumer tech segments.

The Company enforces a proactive IP protection strategy globally. New technologies, unique cosmetic designs, and trademarks are systematically patented and registered with international regulatory registries.

The legal team actively monitors global online and physical marketplaces for unauthorised usage of its assets. The Company pursues formal legal redress against any infringements to defend its market position. Following the acquisition, the Company is integrating its enforcement practices with the legal resources and global patent management frameworks of the Harman Group to further enhance IP security.

Product Quality and Brand Reputation Risk Management

The premium positioning of the Bowers & Wilkins brand relies entirely on the superior acoustic performance, craftsmanship, and reliability of its products. Any systemic quality failures, component defects, or product recalls would cause immediate financial friction, drive up warranty claims, and severely damage the brand's long-term reputation with luxury consumers and trade partners.

The Company manages this risk through a comprehensive framework that integrates rigorous quality assurance (QA) and strict quality control (QC) protocols across the entire product lifecycle. This includes continuous engineering staff training, incoming component inspections, and multi-stage testing at every phase of the
Page 4
 
B & W GROUP LIMITED
 
 
 
STRATEGIC REPORT (CONTINUED)
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31 DECEMBER 2025

manufacturing process, culminating in a 100% final performance and cosmetic audit of finished goods.

The Company’s manufacturing facilities operate under a formal ISO 9001 Quality Management System, which is subject to regular internal and external independent compliance audits. To eliminate downstream quality risks, these rigorous standards are extended to the vendor base; the Company actively deploys its quality audit programmes and performance monitoring systems directly at the supplier level.

Financial and Capital Risk Management

Exposure to liquidity shortfalls and macroeconomic volatility could impair the Company's operational capability or inflate its cost of capital. Specifically, sharp fluctuations across core operating currencies including the US Dollar (USD), Pound Sterling (GBP), Euro (EUR), and Chinese Yuan (CNY) can create volatility in reported revenues, distort the balance sheet valuation of overseas assets, and inflate raw material procurement costs.

The Company’s liquidity, capital structure, and overarching financial risks are managed centrally under the treasury function of the ultimate parent group. Capital requirements and funding movements are monitored through integrated budgeting and rolling forecasting systems to maintain appropriate capital allocation.

To manage liquidity risk, the local management team maintains close reporting links with the parent group’s treasury team. This ensures that accurate, forward-looking cash flow projections are communicated in good time, securing the capital required to meet foreseeable operational obligations and support planned product roadmaps.

Research and Development

The continuous advancement of proprietary technologies and product innovation remains central to maintaining the Company’s competitive advantage and premium positioning within the global audio market. To sustain this technical leadership, the Company maintains a significant and consistent capital commitment to its pipeline, investing 7.4% of continuing revenue in Research and Development ("R&D") during the financial year ended 31 December 2025 (31 December 2024: 5.6%).

Reflecting the long-term commercial value and generation of future economic benefits from these activities, qualifying development costs are capitalised as intangible assets and subsequently amortised in accordance with the Company's accounting policies. The commercial maturation of this sustained R&D investment is evidenced by the successful market introduction of an extensive range of next-generation consumer audio products and acoustic technologies during the subsequent period.

Employee Engagement and Employment Policies

The Company recognises that its workforce is central to its operational excellence and long-term commercial success. In alignment with modern corporate governance standards, the Company maintains structured frameworks to ensure robust engagement, equal opportunity, and professional development:

- Employee Consultation and Engagement: The Company actively keeps employees informed on operational matters, structural updates, and the broader macroeconomic and financial factors influencing the performance of both Bowers & Wilkins and the ultimate parent group. This communication is sustained through regular staff briefings, corporate newsletters, and collaborative digital channels. In line with the parent group's corporate culture, management actively encourages two-way communication, inviting feedback from employees on strategic and workplace issues.
- Diversity, Inclusion, and Equal Opportunities: The Company is committed to employment practices built upon equal opportunity and meritocracy. All employment decisions including recruitment, promotion, and training are conducted irrespective of gender, race, colour, nationality, ethnic origin, disability, age, or sexual orientation.
- Employment of Disabled Persons: Full and fair consideration is given to all applications for employment from disabled persons, directly matching their specific aptitudes and abilities to available roles. Should an
Page 5
 
B & W GROUP LIMITED
 
 
 
STRATEGIC REPORT (CONTINUED)
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31 DECEMBER 2025

existing employee become disabled during their tenure, the Company’s policy is to maintain employment wherever possible, providing comprehensive retraining, workplace adaptations, and continuous occupational health support.
- Training and Human Capital Investment: The Company continues to invest significantly in training and career development programs to build internal talent pipelines and retain specialised engineering expertise. This commitment is supported by active graduate development pathways and formalised apprenticeship schemes operating across the Company's primary business functions.

Section 172 Statement: Duty to Promote the Success of the Company

Pursuant to Section 172(1) of the Companies Act 2006, the Directors act in good faith to promote the success of the Company for the benefit of its members as a whole. In doing so, the Board ensures that its strategic decision-making processes are balanced, long-term focused, and appropriately informed by the following key factors:

• The likely consequences of any decision in the long term;
• The interests of the Company’s employee base;
• The need to foster the Company’s business relationships with suppliers, customers, and partners;
• The impact of the Company’s operations on the community and the environment;
• The desirability of the Company maintaining a reputation for high standards of business conduct; and
• The need to act fairly as between members of the Company.

- Stakeholder Engagement and Board Governance

The Board maintains an open, transparent dialogue with key stakeholders to develop a comprehensive understanding of their evolving needs, evaluate their perspectives, and align their interests with the Company’s strategic ambitions and corporate culture. Before approving any critical operational or capital allocation plans, the Board and its Committees formally evaluate the potential impacts on relevant stakeholders alongside broader environmental, social, and governance (ESG) responsibilities.

The practical application of Section 172 factors is embedded within the daily operations of the business and is illustrated throughout this Strategic Report, specifically within the Board’s approach to:

- Risk Management and Group Alignment: Ensuring long-term business resilience through safety stock buffers, rigorous supplier vetting, and the strategic alignment of corporate governance policies with the Harman International Incorporated framework.
- Research and Development: Sustaining high-margin market leadership through a continuous 7.4% capital investment into next-generation acoustic technologies and product pipelines.
- Environmental Sustainability: Reviewing and auditing operational footprints against strict product compliance directives (RoHS, REACH, WEEE) and energy efficiency regulations (ESOS).
- Employee Involvement: Fostering a progressive, inclusive workplace through two-way communication channels, graduate pathways, and robust apprenticeship programs.

Key Decisions During the Period

Throughout this transitional financial year, notably marked by the full corporate acquisition of the Company by Harman International Industries; the Directors ensured that all structural integration initiatives, joint venture expansions (including partnerships with McLaren Group Ltd and Abbey Road Studios), and operational capital investments were executed under strict adherence to Section 172 guidelines, protecting long-term enterprise value and brand equity.





 
Page 6
 
B & W GROUP LIMITED
 
 
 
STRATEGIC REPORT (CONTINUED)
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31 DECEMBER 2025

Significant Events: Change of Control and Acquisition

On 6 May 2025, a definitive agreement was announced by the Company’s former ultimate parent undertaking to divest its consumer audio business division, which encompasses B & W Group Ltd. and its subsidiary undertakings to HARMAN International Industries, Incorporated (“HARMAN”). HARMAN operates as a standalone, wholly owned subsidiary of Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd..

Following the receipt of required regulatory approvals and the satisfaction of customary closing conditions, this transaction was formally completed on 23 September 2025, at which point absolute ownership of the Company successfully transferred to HARMAN.

The Directors monitored the integration process closely throughout the transition. Based on the terms of the acquisition and subsequent operational directives, the Board confirms that no material changes were made to the Company’s legal structure, or primary strategic objectives during the pre-acquisition window.  

Furthermore, the Directors anticipate no structural alterations or disruptions to the Company's core strategic targets or commercial trajectories in the immediate post-acquisition horizon.

Subsequent Events

During 2026, HARMAN executed an Intellectual Property centralisation exercise, inline with HARMAN’s strategic objectives. This involved transferring the Bowers and Wilkins Intellectual Property rights from the Company, to a subsidiary of DEI Sales Inc, the immediate parent, Sound United LLC for $80,170K on 31st August 2026.


This report was approved by the board on 25 September 2026 and signed on its behalf.

Directors' responsibilities statement

The directors are responsible for preparing the directors’ report, strategic report and the financial statements in accordance with applicable law and regulations.

Company law requires the directors to prepare financial statements for each financial year. Under that law they have elected to prepare the financial statements in accordance with UK adopted international accounting standards and applicable law.

Under Company law the directors must not approve the financial statements unless they are satisfied that they give a true and fair view of the state of affairs of the Company and of the profit or loss of the Company for that year.

In preparing the financial statements, the directors are required to:

∙select suitable accounting policies and then apply them consistently;

∙make judgements and estimates that are reasonable, relevant and reliable;

∙state whether applicable Accounting Standards have been followed, subject to any material departures disclosed and explained in the financial statements;

∙assess the Company’s ability to continue as a going concern, disclosing, as applicable, matters related to going concern; and

∙use the going concern basis of accounting unless they either intend to liquidate the Company or to cease operations, or have no realistic alternative but to do so. .

The directors are responsible for keeping adequate accounting records that are sufficient to show and explain the Company’s transactions and disclose with reasonable accuracy at any time the financial position of the Company and enable them to ensure that the financial statements comply with the Companies Act 2006. They are responsible for such internal controls as they determine is necessary to enable the preparation of financial statements that are free from material misstatement, whether due to fraud or error, and have general responsibility for taking such steps as are reasonably open to them to safeguard the assets of the Company and to prevent and detect fraud and other irregularities.

Principal activity

The Company's principal activity during the year under review included the development, manufacture and wholesale distribution of premium monitor loudspeakers, high-end sound systems, high-performance headphones and related equipment and services. The Company also engaged in licensing activities associated with its products and technologies.

Results and dividends

The loss for the year, after taxation, amounted to $20,404 thousand (2024 - loss $7,976 thousand).

The Directors are not recommending any dividend be paid for the year 31 December 2025 (year ended 31 December 2024 - Nil). 

The Company's results for the year include dividend income of $7,438 thousand received from subsidiary undertakings. This dividend was received as part of a group simplification and subsidiary streamlining initiative and does not form part of the Company's ordinary trading activities.

Opinion


We have audited the financial statements of B & W Group Limited (‘the Company’) for the year ended 31 December 2025 set out on pages 14 to 46, which comprise the statement of profit or loss and other comprehensive income, statement of financial position, statement of changes in equity, statement of cash flows and related notes, including the material accounting policies set out in note 2.

The financial reporting framework that has been applied in their preparation is UK Law and UK adopted international accounting standards.

In our opinion:

∙the financial statements give a true and fair view of the state of the Company’s affairs as at 31 December 2025 and of its loss for the year then ended;

∙the financial statements have been properly prepared in accordance with UK adopted international accounting standards; and

∙the financial statements have been prepared in accordance with the requirements of the Companies Act 2006.


Basis for opinion


We conducted our audit in accordance with International Standards on Auditing (UK) ("ISAs (UK)") and applicable law. Our responsibilities under those standards are further described in the Auditor’s responsibilities for the audit of the financial statements section of our report. We are independent of the Company in accordance with ethical requirements that are relevant to our audit of financial statements in the UK, including the Financial Reporting Council (FRC)’s Ethical Standard, and we have fulfilled our other ethical responsibilities in accordance with these requirements.
 
We believe that the audit evidence we have obtained is sufficient and appropriate to provide a basis for our opinion.
 
Conclusions relating to going concern


The directors have prepared the financial statements on the going concern basis as they do not intend to liquidate the Company or to cease its operations, and as they have concluded that the Company’s financial position means that this is realistic. They have also concluded that there are no material uncertainties that could
have cast significant doubt over its ability to continue as a going concern for at least a year from the date of approval of the financial statements (“the going concern period”).

In our evaluation of the directors' conclusions, we considered the inherent risks to the Company’s business model and analysed how those risks might affect the Company’s financial resources or ability to continue operations over the going concern period. In auditing the financial statements, we have concluded that the directors' use of the going concern basis of accounting in the preparation of the financial statements is appropriate.

Based on the work we have performed, we have not identified any material uncertainties relating to events or conditions that, individually or collectively, may cast significant doubt on the Company’s ability to continue as a going concern for a period of at least twelve months from the date when the financial statements are authorised for issue.

Our responsibilities and the responsibilities of the directors with respect to going concern are described in the relevant sections of this report.

However, as we cannot predict all future events or conditions and as subsequent events may result in outcomes that are inconsistent with judgements that were reasonable at the time they were made, the absence of reference to a material uncertainty in this auditor's report is not a guarantee that the Company will continue in operation.

Detecting irregularities including fraud

We identified the areas of laws and regulations that could reasonably be expected to have a material effect on the financial statements and risks of material misstatement due to fraud, using our understanding of the entity's industry, regulatory environment and other external factors and inquiry with the directors. In addition, our risk assessment procedures included: inquiring with the directors as to the Company’s policies and procedures regarding compliance with laws and regulations and prevention and detection of fraud; inquiring whether the directors have knowledge of any actual or suspected non-compliance with laws or regulations or alleged fraud; inspecting the Company’s regulatory and legal correspondence; and reading Board minutes.

We discussed identified laws and regulations, fraud risk factors and the need to remain alert among the audit team.

The Company is subject to laws and regulations that directly affect the financial statements including companies and financial reporting legislation. We assessed the extent of compliance with these laws and regulations as part of our procedures on the related financial statement items, including assessing the financial statement disclosures and agreeing them to supporting documentation when necessary. 

The Company is subject to many other laws and regulations where the consequences of non-compliance could have a material effect on amounts or disclosures in the financial statements, for instance through the imposition of fines or litigation. We identified the following areas as those most likely to have such an effect: health and safety, anti-bribery, employment law, environmental law.

Auditing standards limit the required audit procedures to identify non-compliance with these non-direct laws and regulations to inquiry of the directors and inspection of regulatory and legal correspondence, if any. These limited procedures did not identify actual or suspected non-compliance.  

We assessed events or conditions that could indicate an incentive or pressure to commit fraud or provide an opportunity to commit fraud. As required by auditing standards, we performed procedures to address the risk of management override of controls. On this audit we do not believe there is a fraud risk related to revenue recognition. We did not identify any additional fraud risks.

In response to the risk(s) of fraud, we also performed procedures including: identifying journal entries to test based on risk criteria and comparing the identified entries to supporting documentation; evaluating the business purpose of significant unusual transactions; assessing significant accounting estimates for bias; and assessing the disclosures in the financial statements.

Owing to the inherent limitations of an audit, there is an unavoidable risk that we may not have detected some material misstatements in the financial statements, even though we have properly planned and performed our audit in accordance with auditing standards. For example, the further removed non-compliance with laws and regulations (irregularities) is from the events and transactions reflected in the financial statements, the less likely the inherently limited procedures required by auditing standards would identify it. 

In addition, as with any audit, there remains a higher risk of non-detection of irregularities, as these may involve collusion, forgery, intentional omissions, misrepresentations, or the override of internal controls. We are not responsible for preventing non-compliance and cannot be expected to detect non-compliance with all laws and regulations.

Basis of preparation

The financial statements have been prepared in accordance with International Financial Reporting Standards, International Accounting Standards and Interpretations as adopted by the UK (collectively IFRSs). They were authorised for issue by the Company's board of directors on 25 September 2026.

Details of the Company's accounting policies, including changes during the year, are included in note 2.

In preparing these financial statements, management has made judgments, estimates and assumptions that affect the application of the Company accounting policies and the reported amounts of assets, liabilities, income and expenses. Actual results may differ from these estimates.

Estimates and underlying assumptions are reviewed on an ongoing basis. Revisions to estimates are recognised prospectively.

The areas where judgments and estimates have been made in preparing the financial statements and their effects are disclosed in note 2.16.

During the year, the Company reviewed the classification and presentation of certain balances within the financial statements. As a result, certain comparative amounts have been re-presented to align with the current year presentation. The reclassifications and presentation changes had no impact on previously reported profit for the year, net assets or shareholders' funds.

The Company is exempt from the requirement to prepare consolidated financial statements under section 401 of the Companies Act 2006. Accordingly, these financial statements present information about the Company as an individual undertaking and not about its group. The Company and its subsidiary undertakings are included in the publicly available consolidated financial statements of Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd.


1.1 Basis of measurement

The financial statements have been prepared on the historical cost basis unless otherwise disclosed.

B & W GROUP LIMITED
 
 
 
NOTES TO THE FINANCIAL STATEMENTS
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31 DECEMBER 2025

2.Accounting policies


2.1

Going concern

On 23 September 2025, the Company was acquired by Harman International Industries, Incorporated. Following the acquisition, the Company's day-to-day working capital requirements continue to be funded through operational cash flows without the need for external borrowings.

As at 31 December 2025, the Company maintained a strong liquidity position, reporting net current assets of $48.1 million, which included cash and cash equivalents of $8.2 million. The Company remains debt-free and holds sufficient cash reserves to meet its foreseeable working capital and capital investment requirements. Furthermore, through intercompany pooling arrangements, the Company is a net contributor to the group treasury and holds material net receivables from group undertakings (as detailed in Note 19), which can be recalled supporting working capital if required.

Trading performance remained stable throughout the financial year ended 31 December 2025. Management anticipates growth in the financial year 2026, driven by robust global demand for the Company’s products, the scheduled launch of the flagship Bowers & Wilkins 800 Series, and the ongoing partnership with a high-profile brand ambassador. While gross margins remain dependent on transfer pricing arrangements established by the ultimate parent undertaking, management is satisfied that these mechanisms ensure the Company generates sufficient cash from its operations.

The Directors have assessed the future cash flows of the business by reviewing financial forecasts and considering severe but plausible downside scenarios. Based on this review, management has a reasonable expectation that the Company has adequate resources, including the availability of intercompany receivables, to continue in operational existence for a period of at least 12 months from the date of approval of these financial statements. Accordingly, the Directors have not identified any material uncertainties that may cast significant doubt upon the Company’s ability to continue as a going concern, and they continue to adopt the going concern basis in preparing the financial statements.

 
2.2

Revenue

Revenue is measured based on the consideration specified in a contract with a customer and excludes amounts collected on behalf of third parties. The Company recognises revenue when it transfers control over a product or service to a customer.

The Company does not expect to have any contracts where the period between the transfer of the promised goods or services to the customer and payment by the customer exceeds one year. As a consequence, the Company does not adjust any of the transaction prices for the time value of money.

Page 22
 
B & W GROUP LIMITED
 
 
 
NOTES TO THE FINANCIAL STATEMENTS
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31 DECEMBER 2025

2.Accounting policies (continued)

  
2.3

Leasing


The Company as a lessee

The Company assesses whether a contract is or contains a lease, at inception of a contract. The Company recognises a right-of-use asset and a corresponding lease liability with respect to all lease agreements in which it is the lessee, except for short-term leases (defined as leases with a lease term of 12 months or less) and leases of low-value assets. For these leases, the Company recognises the lease payments as an operating expense on a straight-line basis over the term of the lease unless another systematic basis is more representative of the time pattern in which economic benefits from the leased asset are consumed.

The lease liability is initially measured at the present value of the lease payments that are not paid at the commencement date, discounted by using the rate implicit in the lease. If this rate cannot be readily determined, the Company uses its incremental borrowing rate. The incremental borrowing rate is determined by reference to the Bank of England base rate, with an additional margin of 3%. This margin reflects the Company's assessment of the cost of obtaining secured borrowing over a similar term and with similar economic characteristics, taking into account prevailing market conditions and changes in the cost of capital.

Lease payments included in the measurement of the lease liability comprise:

∙fixed lease payments (including in-substance fixed payments), less any lease incentives;


The lease liability is included in the 'Loans and borrowings' line in the Statement of financial position.

The lease liability is subsequently measured by increasing the carrying amount to reflect interest on the lease liability (using the effective interest method) and by reducing the carrying amount to reflect the lease payments made.

The right-of-use assets comprise the initial measurement of the corresponding lease liability, lease payments made at or before the commencement day and any initial direct costs. They are subsequently measured at cost less accumulated depreciation and impairment losses.

Right-of-use assets are depreciated over the shorter period of lease term and useful life of the underlying asset. If a lease transfers ownership of the underlying asset or the cost of the right-of-use asset reflects that the Company expects to exercise a purchase option, the related right-of-use asset is depreciated over the useful life of the underlying asset. The depreciation starts at the commencement date of the lease.

The right-of-use assets are included in the 'Property, Plant and Equipment' lines, as applicable, in the Statement of financial position.

The Company applies IAS 36 to determine whether a right-of-use asset is impaired and accounts for any identified impairment loss as described in note 2.7.

As a practical expedient, IFRS 16 permits a lessee not to separate non-lease components, and instead account for any lease and associated non-lease components as a single arrangement. The Company has used this practical expedient.

2.Accounting policies (continued)

 
2.4

Foreign currency

In preparing the financial statements of each individual group entity, transactions in currencies other than the entity's functional currency (foreign currencies) are recognised at the rates of exchange prevailing at the dates of the transactions. At the end of each reporting period, monetary items denominated in foreign currencies are retranslated at the rates prevailing at that date. Non-monetary items carried at fair value that are denominated in foreign currencies are retranslated at the rates prevailing at the date when the fair value was determined. Non-monetary items that are measured in terms of historical cost in a foreign currency are not retranslated.

Exchange differences on monetary items are recognised in profit or loss in the period in which they arise except for:
∙exchange differences on foreign currency borrowings relating to assets under construction for future productive use, which are included in the cost of those assets when they are regarded as an adjustment to interest costs on those foreign currency borrowings;
∙exchange differences on transactions entered into in order to hedge certain foreign currency risks (see  for hedging accounting policies); and
∙exchange differences on monetary items receivable from or payable to foreign operation for which settlement is neither planned nor likely to occur (therefore forming part of the net investment in the foreign operation), which are recognised initially in other comprehensive income and reclassified from equity to profit or loss on repayment of the monetary items.

For the purposes of presenting these financial statements, the assets and liabilities of the Company's foreign operations are translated into USD using exchange rates prevailing at the end of each reporting period. Income and expense items are translated at the average exchange rates for the period, unless exchange rates fluctuate significantly during that period, in which case the exchange rates at the dates of the transactions are used. Exchange differences arising, if any, are recognised in other comprehensive income and accumulated in equity (and attributed to non-controlling interests as appropriate).

On the disposal of a foreign operation (i.e. a disposal of the Company's entire interest in a foreign operation, a disposal involving loss of control over a subsidiary that includes a foreign operation, or a partial disposal of an interest in a joint arrangement or an associate that includes a foreign operation of which the retained interest becomes a financial asset), all of the exchange differences accumulated in equity in respect of that operation attributable to the owners of the Company are reclassified to profit or loss.

In addition, in relation to a partial disposal of a subsidiary that includes a foreign operation that does not result in the Group losing control over the subsidiary, the proportionate share of accumulated exchange differences are re-attributed to non-controlling interests and are not recognised in profit or loss. For all other partial disposals (i.e. partial disposals of associates or joint arrangements that do not result in the Group losing significant influence or joint control), the proportionate share of the accumulated exchange differences is reclassified to profit or loss.

2.Accounting policies (continued)


2.5

Borrowing costs

Borrowing costs directly attributable to the acquisition, construction or production of qualifying assets, which are assets that necessarily take a substantial period of time to get ready for their intended use or sale, are added to the cost of those assets, until such time as the assets are substantially ready for their intended use or sale.

Investment income earned on the temporary investment of specific borrowings pending their expenditure on qualifying assets is deducted from the borrowing costs eligible for capitalisation.

All other borrowing costs are recognised in profit or loss in the period in which they are incurred.

 
2.6

Taxation


(i) Current tax

The tax currently payable is based on taxable profit for the year. Taxable profit differs from ‘profit before tax’ as reported in the Statement of profit or loss and other comprehensive income because of items of income or expense that are taxable or deductible in other years and items that are never taxable or deductible. The Company's current tax is calculated using tax rates that have been enacted or substantively enacted by the end of the reporting period.

NOTES TO THE FINANCIAL STATEMENTS
FOR THE YEAR ENDED 31 DECEMBER 2025

2.Accounting policies (continued)


2.6
Taxation (continued)


(ii) Deferred tax

Deferred tax is recognised on temporary differences between the carrying amounts of assets and liabilities in the financial statements and the corresponding tax bases used in the computation of taxable profit. Deferred tax liabilities are generally recognised for all taxable temporary differences. Deferred tax assets are generally recognised for all deductible temporary differences to the extent that it is probable that taxable profits will be available against which those deductible temporary differences can be utilised. Such deferred tax assets and liabilities are not recognised if the temporary difference arises from the initial recognition (other than in a business combination) of assets and liabilities in a transaction that affects neither the taxable profit nor the accounting profit. In addition, deferred tax liabilities are not recognised if the temporary difference arises from the initial recognition of goodwill.

Deferred tax liabilities are recognised for taxable temporary differences associated with investments in subsidiaries and associates, and interests in joint ventures, except where the Company is able to control the reversal of the temporary difference and it is probable that the temporary difference will not reverse in the foreseeable future. Deferred tax assets arising from deductible temporary differences associated with such investments and interests are only recognised to the extent that it is probable that there will be sufficient taxable profits against which to utilise the benefits of the temporary differences and they are expected to reverse in the foreseeable future.

The carrying amount of deferred tax assets is reviewed at the end of each reporting period and reduced to the extent that it is no longer probable that sufficient taxable profits will be available to allow all or part of the asset to be recovered.

Deferred tax liabilities and assets are measured at the tax rates that are expected to apply in the period in which the liability is settled or the asset realised, based on tax rates (and tax laws) that have been enacted or substantively enacted by the end of the reporting period.

The measurement of deferred tax liabilities and assets reflects the tax consequences that would follow from the manner in which the Company expects, at the end of the reporting period, to recover or settle the carrying amount of its assets and liabilities.

International tax reform - Pillar Two model rules

The Company has applied the mandatory exception to the recognition and disclosure of information about deferred tax assets and liabilities related to Pillar Two income taxes (i.e. income taxes arising from the jurisdictional implementation of OECD’s Pillar Two Model Rules).


(iii) Current and deferred tax for the year

Current and deferred tax are recognised in profit or loss, except when they relate to items that are recognised in other comprehensive income or directly in equity, in which case, the current and deferred tax are also recognised in other comprehensive income or directly in equity respectively. Where current tax or deferred tax arises from the initial accounting for a business combination, the tax effect is included in the accounting for the business combination.

2.7

Property, plant and equipment

Items of property, plant and equipment are measured at cost less accumulated depreciation and any accumulated impairment losses.

If significant parts of an item of property, plant and equipment have different useful lives, then they are accounted for as separate items (major components) of property, plant and equipment. Any gain or loss on disposal of an item of property, plant and equipment is recognised in profit or loss. Subsequent expenditure is capitalised only if it is probable that the future economic benefits associated with the expenditure will flow to the Company.

Depreciation is provided on all other items of property, plant and equipment so as to write off their carrying value over their expected useful economic lives. It is provided at the following range:

2.8

Intangible assets


(i) Intangible assets acquired separately

Intangible assets with finite useful lives that are acquired separately are carried at cost less accumulated amortisation and accumulated impairment losses. Amortisation of intellectual property is recognised on a straight-line basis over their estimated useful lives. Capitalised development costs are amortised over the expected economic life of the related product. The expected economic life is determined by estimating the product's lifetime sales, based on management's assessment of forecast demand and historical sales performance of comparable products within the same category.

The estimated useful life and amortisation method are reviewed at the end of each reporting period, with the effect of any changes in estimate being accounted for on a prospective basis. Intangible assets with indefinite useful lives that are acquired separately are carried at cost less accumulated impairment losses.

2.Accounting policies (continued)


2.8
Intangible assets (continued)


(ii) Internally-generated intangible assets

Expenditure on research activities is recognised as an expense in the period in which it is incurred.

An internally-generated intangible asset arising from development (or from the development phase of an internal project) is recognised if, and only if, all of the following have been demonstrated:

∙the technical feasibility of completing the intangible asset so that it will be available for use or sale;
∙the intention to complete the intangible asset and use or sell it;
∙the ability to use or sell the intangible asset;
∙how the intangible asset will generate probable future economic benefits;
∙the availability of adequate technical, financial and other resources to complete the development and to use or sell the intangible asset; and
∙the ability to measure reliably the expenditure attributable to the intangible asset during its development.

The amount initially recognised for internally-generated intangible assets is the sum of the expenditure incurred from the date when the intangible asset first meets the recognition criteria listed above. Where no internally-generated intangible asset can be recognised, development expenditure is recognised in profit or loss in the period in which it is incurred.

Subsequent to initial recognition, internally-generated intangible assets are reported at cost less accumulated amortisation and accumulated impairment losses, on the same basis as intangible assets that are acquired separately.

 
2.9

Inventories

Inventories are stated at the lower of cost and net realisable value. Costs of inventories are determined on a first in, first out basis. Net realisable value represents the estimated selling price for inventories less all estimated costs of completion and costs necessary to make the sale.


2.10

Cash and cash equivalents

Cash and cash equivalents comprise cash on hand and demand deposits, together with other short-term, highly liquid investments maturing within 90 days from the date of acquisition that are readily convertible into known amounts of cash and which are subject to an insignificant risk of changes in value.


2.11

Employee benefits

Employee benefits comprise wages and salaries, paid annual leave, bonuses, pension contributions, medical insurance, life insurance and other benefits provided to employees in exchange for services rendered.

2.Accounting policies (continued)

 
2.12

Provisions

Provisions are recognised when the Company has a present obligation (legal or constructive) as a result of a past event, it is probable that the Company will be required to settle the obligation, and a reliable estimate can be made of the amount of the obligation.

The amount recognised as a provision is the best estimate of the consideration required to settle the present obligation at the end of the reporting period, taking into account the risks and uncertainties surrounding the obligation. When a provision is measured using the cash flows estimated to settle the present obligation, its carrying amount is the present value of those cash flows (when the effect of the time value of money is material).

When some or all of the economic benefits required to settle a provision are expected to be recovered from a third party, a receivable is recognised as an asset if it is virtually certain that reimbursement will be received and the amount of the receivable can be measured reliably.


2.13

Investments

Investments in subsidiaries are carried at cost less any accumulated impairment losses.


2.14

Impairment

At each reporting date, the Company assesses whether there is any indication that a non-financial asset may be impaired. Where an indicator exists, the recoverable amount is estimated as the higher of fair value less costs of disposal and value in use. An impairment loss is recognised in profit or loss where the carrying amount exceeds the recoverable amount.


2.15

Finance income/expense

Finance income comprises interest income on cash deposits and other financial assets, recognised using the effective interest method.

Finance expense comprises interest expense on borrowings, lease liabilities and other financing costs. Borrowing costs that are not directly attributable to the acquisition, construction or production of a qualifying asset are recognised in profit or loss using the effective interest method.


2.16

Significant judgements and estimates

The preparation of the financial statements requires management to make judgements, estimates and assumptions that affect the application of accounting policies and the reported amounts of assets, liabilities, income and expenses. Actual results may differ from these estimates.
 
Estimates and underlying assumptions are reviewed on an ongoing basis. Revisions to accounting estimates are recognised prospectively in the period of the revision and in any future periods affected.
 
The principal areas involving significant judgement and estimation are set out in the relevant notes to the financial statements. These include the recognition and measurement of deferred tax assets and liabilities, provisions, impairment of R&D assets, and investment impairment.

2.18

Financial instruments

Financial assets and financial liabilities are recognised when an entity becomes a party to the contractual provisions of the instruments.

Financial assets and financial liabilities are initially measured at fair value. Transaction costs that are directly attributable to the acquisition or issue of financial assets and financial liabilities (other than financial assets and financial liabilities at fair value through profit or loss) are added to or deducted from the fair value of the financial assets or financial liabilities, as appropriate, on initial recognition. Transaction costs directly attributable to the acquisition of financial assets or financial liabilities at fair value through profit or loss are recognised immediately in profit or loss.

2.19

Financial risk management

The Company finances its operations through retained cash reserves and drawing on debts from related parties, the company has no external borrowings.

Liquidity risk

The Company has significant receivables from other companies within the Group. These amounts are available to be drawn down as and when required and, as a result, management considers the Company to have sufficient liquidity to meet its obligations as they fall due.

Foreign exchange risk

The Company is exposed to the effects of changes in foreign currency exchange rates on its financial position and cash flows.

The Company is exposed to foreign currency risk in respect of transactions and balances denominated in currencies other than USD.
 
The Company’s principal foreign currency exposure arises from significant amounts receivable from related parties, which are denominated in currencies other than USD. The Company also has exposure to foreign currency risk in respect of third-party trade and other payables denominated in currencies other than USD.
 
Foreign exchange movements may result in gains or losses on the retranslation and settlement of these monetary balances. The Company monitors its foreign currency exposures on an ongoing basis and considers the level of exposure when managing intercompany balances and settlements.
 
Management considers the Company’s exposure to foreign currency risk to be manageable, although movements in exchange rates could have a material impact on the Company’s reported results.


3.


Reporting entity

B & W Group Ltd (the 'Company') is a limited company incorporated in the United Kingdom. The Company's registered office is at Dale Road, Worthing, West Sussex BN11 2BH. The Company's principal activity is to development, manufacture of premium monitor loudspeakers, high-end sound systems, high-performance headphones and related equipment and services. The Company also engaged in licensing activities associated with its products and technologies.


4.

These financial statements are presented in US dollars, which is the Company's functional currency. All amounts have been rounded to the nearest thousand, unless otherwise indicated.

27.


Reserves


Share premium

The share premium reserve represents the amount paid for shares in excess of their nominal values. This reserve is non-distributable.

Other reserves

This comprises the foreign currency reserve established at the date that the functional currency was changed to USD as of 1 October 2014.

Retained earnings

The retained earnings account comprises the balance of profits accumulated over the life of the Company.

29.


Controlling party

DEI Sales Inc. of 5541 Fermi Ct., Carlsbad, CA 92008, United States acquired B & W Group Ltd.
on 9 October 2020 and their parent company became Viper Holdings Corporation, (trading as
Sound United) of 54th Floor, 200 Clarendon Street, Boston, Massachusetts.

On the 23rd September 2025, Viper Holdings Corporation of which B & W Group Ltd. and its subsidiaries
are part, was acquired by Harman International Industries, Incorporated, a company ultimately owned by Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd. a publicly traded company located 129 Samsung-ro Maetan-3dong, Suwon-si, Gyeonggido, South Korea.

The largest and smallest group that prepares consolidated financial statements that include the
results and financial position of the Company, is that headed by Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd.

Pension commitments

Employees may belong to a personal pension plan or money purchase scheme (defined
contribution schemes). The assets of the schemes are administered in funds independent of
those of the Company.

payable to the schemes of $1,908,000 for the Company (2024:$1,765,000). At 31 December
2025, the Company owed $237,000 (2024: $199,000) to pension schemes.

32.


Contingent liabilities

The Company has guaranteed the period end liabilities of B & W Group (Logistics) Ltd. (Company number 05259045) and B & W Loudspeakers Ltd (04890501) under section 479A of the Companies Act 2006 and as such the subsidiary has taken advantage of the audit exemption. B & W Group (Logistics) Ltd was liquidated on 20th April 2026.


33.


Capital Commitments

The Company's financing is managed as part of the ultimate parent's treasury function against
an objective to consistently reduce borrowings through profitable trading and strong working
capital management whilst permitting capital investments necessary for long term growth.
The Company is not subject to any externally imposed capital requirements.


34.

Events after the reporting date

During 2026, HARMAN executed an Intellectual Property centralisation exercise, inline with HARMAN’s strategic objectives. This involved transferring the Bowers and Wilkins Intellectual Property rights from the Company, to a subsidiary of DEI Sales Inc, the immediate parent, Sound United LLC for $80,170K on 31st August 2026.
